The eggs of the Great tit (Parus major), when incubated at a stable temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], typically hatch after an incubation period of approximately 13.8 days [ab = approximately 13.8 days], a duration that aligns closely with predictions from comparative analyses of altricial bird development. Upon hatching, the newly emerged nestlings are remarkably small, with a reported wet weight at birth of just 1.3 grams [Wwb = 1.3 grams]. This minimal initial mass reflects the altricial state of the hatchlings, which are completely dependent on their parents for thermoregulation and feeding. The first few days of life are characterized by rapid growth fueled by frequent provisioning, as both parents work tirelessly to meet the energetic demands of the brood. This brief but critical incubation phase, measured under controlled laboratory conditions replicating natural nest temperatures, underscores the precision of the species' developmental timing, a trait that has been well documented in the literature on European parid life history.

During the nestling period, the altricial chicks of the Great tit undergo a dramatic transformation. At approximately 19 days after hatching [tx = approximately 19 days after hatching], and given the high body temperatures typical of an active, endothermic nestling (41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]), the young birds achieve fledging, a milestone marked by their first sustained flight and departure from the nest cavity. The fledging process is a critical transition, requiring significant muscle and feather development. Subsequently, the period leading up to sexual maturity is also temperature-dependent. Under similar thermal conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], which represents the core body temperature of an active adult, the post-fledging juveniles experience a period of gonadal development. The attainment of puberty, defined by the ability to produce gametes, occurs approximately 57 days after hatching [tp = approximately 57 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively rapid maturation for a small passerine allows individuals to potentially breed in the calendar year following their birth.

The ultimate wet weight of a sexually mature adult female Great tit stabilizes around 17.9 grams [Wwi = around 17.9 grams], a figure that represents the typical asymptotic mass for this sex. Adult males, however, tend to be slightly heavier, achieving a ultimate wet weight of approximately 19.05 grams [Wwi = approximately 19.05 grams]. This modest sexual size dimorphism is common among small passerines and is thought to relate to differences in competitive behavior and metabolic demands during the breeding season. The adult body mass is a plastic trait that fluctuates seasonally, with birds accumulating fat reserves during winter to survive cold nights and depleting them during the energetically costly breeding season. Field studies have shown that the maximum recorded lifespan for these birds, which is dependent on the high metabolic and body temperatures characteristic of endotherms (41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]), can reach up to 5475 days [am = up to 5475 days], or approximately 15 years, a remarkable longevity for an animal of its small size.

The onset of first reproduction is a pivotal event in the life cycle of any organism. The maximum reproductive rate, observed under optimal conditions with abundant food and at the elevated metabolic body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], is considerable. The species is capable of laying up to 18 eggs in a single clutch [N_R_i = up to 18 eggs in a single clutch], though the species typically achieves a maximum of only one successful brood per year [F_R_i = one successful brood per year]. Brood size is highly variable, often correlating with the abundance of winter moth caterpillars, their primary nestling food source.

In addition to their intrinsic life-history traits, Great tits exhibit fascinating behavioral plasticity that influences their survival. Their ability to learn and adapt to novel food sources, such as opening milk bottles to drink cream, is a classic example of cultural evolution in birds. Cognitive studies have shown that individuals with larger spatial memory capacities are more efficient at caching and retrieving food, a crucial skill for surviving unpredictable winter conditions. From a physiological standpoint, their basal metabolic rate is exceptionally high, a necessity for maintaining their elevated core body temperature against the cold European winters. The interplay between their cognitive abilities, metabolic demands, and the life-history constraints described previously makes Parus major a cornerstone species for studies in evolutionary ecology and behavioral genetics.
